title: I Asked My Upstairs Neighbor Three Times to Stop Tossing Used Tea Bags Onto My Balcony—Then I Discovered Why

blocks.text: I had lived in apartment 3B for almost eight years, and in all that time, I had learned one important rule about apartment living:
You could survive almost anything if you were willing to be patient.
A neighbor who thought Sunday morning was the perfect time to rearrange furniture.
Even the occasional cigarette smell drifting through an open window.
But there was one thing I couldn’t tolerate.
Used tea bags being thrown onto my balcony.
It started so innocently that I didn’t even think twice.
One Saturday morning, I stepped outside to water my plants and noticed a damp tea bag lying beside one of my flowerpots.
I assumed the wind had carried it over from somewhere.
I picked it up, threw it away, and forgot about it.
One usually landed around seven in the morning.
Another appeared sometime around nine at night.
Then one afternoon, I hung a freshly washed white towel over a chair on my balcony.
When I came back outside, a wet tea bag was sitting directly on top of it.
Brown liquid had soaked through the fabric.
He was in his early forties and had always seemed relatively harmless. We weren’t friends, but we’d exchanged polite greetings in the hallway plenty of times.
After a few seconds, he opened the door.
“Evan, I’ve found these all over my balcony.”
“That doesn’t explain why you’re throwing the bags onto my balcony.”
The next morning, at 7:03, another tea bag landed beside my basil plant.
But the following night, another appeared.
Three weeks later, another tea bag landed on my balcony.
That laugh bothered me more than the tea bags.
“You live downstairs,” he said. “Where else is it supposed to go?”
“You’re making a huge deal out of nothing.”
But something about the whole situation felt wrong.
And they appeared at almost exactly the same times every day.
I began watching from behind my curtains.
At 6:55 one morning, I stood inside my living room.
The next morning, instead of throwing the tea bag away, I put it into a small plastic bag.
After a week, I had fourteen tea bags sitting in a sealed container in my kitchen.
One morning, I found a tea bag on my balcony before 7 a.m.
My hands started shaking as I unfolded it.
There were only four words written on it:
I immediately looked toward apartment 4B.
Someone had deliberately attached that message to the tea bag.
Evan opened the door almost immediately.
The moment he saw the paper in my hand, the color drained from his face.
“Because whoever left that wants you to think I’m responsible.”
“I’ve been trying to keep you from noticing something.”
“Because I needed you to believe I was the one throwing them.”
“Why would you want me to believe that?”
From his apartment, I could see my balcony perfectly.
There was a tiny black object attached underneath it.
“I found one on my balcony three months ago.”
He reached into a drawer and pulled out a small envelope.
Pictures taken from angles that made my skin crawl.
“Because the person watching us wanted us to fight.”
“The tea bags started after I discovered the first camera. I realized someone was using them to make you angry with me.”
It showed me standing on my balcony, holding a cup of coffee.
My voice came out barely above a whisper.
Then Evan said something that made my blood run cold.
“Those are the times the cameras activate.”
We spent the next hour checking every window, railing, vent, and light fixture in my apartment.
One of the flowerpots on my balcony had been moved.
Underneath the flowerpot was a small metal box.
Someone had been watching me for months.
The video showed my balcony at exactly 9:00 p.m.
